message: Untracked files inside this commit's scope are silently excluded (exit 0, no warning). Naming the file directly errors; naming its directory doesn't. Run `git status` or check `git show --name-only HEAD`.
This path has nothing staged or modified — it contributes nothing to the commit. Confirm it's the one you meant.
This pathspec matches no files — nothing will be staged, and git won't say so. Check the path and working directory.
Every file this pathspec matches is ignored, so nothing will be staged. Use `git add -f` if intended.
`add -u` stages tracked modifications only; any new file in this change will be left behind.
Restoring this staged path's working tree leaves the index copy in place — it looks reverted while a stale version stays staged. Add `--staged` to clear both.
Restoring from a ref writes the index as well as the working tree, staging this content without an add. Check `git diff --cached` before committing.
A one-sided strategy resolves every conflict automatically and reports a clean result — the discarded side is never shown, indistinguishable from a conflict-free merge.
This path differs from a tracked file only by case, and the filesystem folds case: git resolves to the existing path, so the rename silently fails.
This path passes through a clean filter, so committed content differs from disk. The working copy won't show what you're committing — use `git show HEAD:<path>` to see the committed form.
The working tree has modifications, and `reset --hard` destroys them unrecoverably (the reflog protects commits, never uncommitted work). Stash first, or run `git status` to see what's at risk.
This clean would delete files — with `-x`, even what gitignore protects, like dependency trees and databases. `git clean -n` with the same flags previews the exact list.
This branch holds commits not merged into HEAD — exactly what `-d` refuses and `-D` bypasses. Note the branch tip SHA first: after deletion, only the reflog gets you back.
Stash entries exist, and `stash clear` discards all unrecoverably. `git stash list` shows what's about to drop; `stash drop` removes one entry by name instead.
Immediate expiry deletes the reflog safety net every git recovery relies on — dropped commits and resets are then gone for good.
This push deletes a ref on the remote — destructive at a distance, invisible locally. Confirm the branch name and that nobody else's work rides on it.

Plain `--force` overwrites the remote even if someone pushed after you last fetched; `--force-with-lease` fails instead — the entire difference between rewriting your own history and destroying someone else's.
